items.title: Babur & the Foundation of the Mughal Empire (1526-1530)
items.body:
**In one line:** Babur, a Central Asian prince descended from Timur and Genghis Khan, founded the Mughal Empire by winning the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.

**The story**

- **Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur** (born 1483 at Andijan in Ferghana) was a **descendant of Timur** (father's side) and **Genghis/Chinggis Khan** (mother's side), so he inherited the Timurid claim.
- After losing his Central Asian homelands (Samarqand, Ferghana), he captured **Kabul in 1504** and used it as a base to march into Hindustan.
- At **Panipat (1526)**, though heavily outnumbered, he beat Ibrahim Lodi using **field artillery** and the Ottoman (Rumi) **tulughma / linked-cart** tactic he had learnt about from the battle of Chaldiran (1514).
- Three more wins secured north India; he died at Agra in **1530** and was succeeded by his son **Humayun**.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** The founder, the four battles with years, Babur's lineage and the Baburnama are the standard Prelims facts for Mughal origins.

**Picture it — the four decisive battles**

| Battle | Year | Opponent | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **First Panipat** | 1526 | Ibrahim Lodi (Delhi Sultan) | Ended the Lodi/Delhi Sultanate; founded Mughal rule |
| **Khanwa** | 1527 | Rana Sanga (Mewar) | Broke the Rajput confederacy; consolidated N. India |
| **Chanderi** | 1528 | Medini Rai (Malwa) | Captured Chanderi (Rajputs performed jauhar) |
| **Ghaghra** | 1529 | Afghan confederacy | Secured the east (Bihar/Bengal frontier) |

**Terms explained**

- **Timurid** = descended from Timur (Tamerlane), the 14th-century Central Asian conqueror.
- **tulughma / linked-cart (araba)** = tying carts together with gaps for guns, making a mobile shield-wall; artillery fires through the gaps.
- **jauhar** = Rajput practice of mass self-immolation by women to avoid capture.
- **Baburnama (Tuzuk-i-Baburi)** = Babur's own memoirs, written in **Chagatai Turkish**.
- **Charbagh** = a four-part Persian garden (Babur's Aram Bagh / Ram Bagh at Agra).

**Don't confuse:** The **First** Battle of Panipat (1526, Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi) with the **Second** (1556, Akbar's regent Bairam Khan vs Hemu) and the **Third** (1761, Marathas vs Ahmad Shah Abdali) — three different battles on the same field.

**Remember it:** Babur's battles "P-K-C-G" = Panipat, Khanwa, Chanderi, Ghaghra (1526-27-28-29).

**TL;DR**

- Babur, descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, founded the Mughal Empire in 1526.
- First Panipat (1526) ended the Delhi Sultanate; Khanwa (1527), Chanderi (1528), Ghaghra (1529) followed.
- He used artillery and the tulughma (linked-cart) tactic to beat larger armies.
- Wrote the Baburnama in Chagatai Turkish; introduced Charbagh gardens; died 1530.
keyPoints: Babur, descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, founded the Mughal Empire in 1526.
First Battle of Panipat (1526) defeated Ibrahim Lodi and ended the Delhi Sultanate.
Battle of Khanwa (1527) defeated Rana Sanga; Chanderi (1528) and Ghaghra (1529) followed.
Babur used artillery and the tulughma (linked-cart) tactic to beat larger armies.
He wrote the Baburnama (Tuzuk-i-Baburi) in Chagatai Turkish and introduced Charbagh gardens.

items.title: Humayun & the Sur Interregnum (Sher Shah Suri)
items.body:
**In one line:** Humayun lost the throne to the brilliant Afghan administrator Sher Shah Suri, spent 15 years in exile, and won it back in 1555 — just before dying.

**The story**

- **Humayun** (ruled 1530-40, then 1555-56) weakened himself early by **dividing the empire among his brothers** (Kamran, Askari, Hindal).
- The Afghan **Sher Shah Suri** beat him at **Chausa (1539)** and **Kannauj/Bilgram (1540)**; Humayun fled into **15 years of exile in Safavid Persia**, sheltered by **Shah Tahmasp**.
- Sher Shah then ruled for just five years (**1540-45**) but reformed revenue, coinage and roads so effectively that Humayun himself called him **'Ustad-i-Badshahan' (Teacher of Kings)**. His work became the **base for Akbar's administration** and later British revenue systems.
- Humayun **recaptured Delhi in 1555** (battles of Machhiwara and Sirhind) and died in **1556** after a fall from his library stairs. His widow built **Humayun's Tomb** — India's **first garden tomb** and a model for the Taj Mahal.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** Sher Shah's reforms (rupiya, GT Road, patta/kabuliyat) are among the most-asked administrative facts of the whole medieval syllabus.

**Picture it — Sher Shah's reforms**

| Area | Reform |
|---|---|
| Revenue | sarkars → parganas; land measured & classified; state share **one-third**; **patta** (title deed) + **kabuliyat** (agreement) |
| Coinage | standardised the **silver rupiya** and **copper dam** |
| Roads | restored the **Grand Trunk Road** with **sarais** (inns) |
| Military | revived **dagh** (branding horses) and **chehra** (soldier roll) from Alauddin Khalji |

**Terms explained**

- **interregnum** = a gap between two spells of one dynasty's rule (here the Sur rule between Humayun's two reigns).
- **patta** = a document stating a peasant's holding and dues; **kabuliyat** = the peasant's written agreement to pay.
- **sarai** = a roadside inn for travellers and traders.
- **rupiya** = Sher Shah's silver coin, ancestor of today's rupee.

**Don't confuse:** **Sher Shah Suri** (Afghan, Sur dynasty) was *not* a Mughal — he interrupted Mughal rule. **Humayun's Tomb** (first garden tomb) is distinct from the later Taj Mahal it inspired.

**Remember it:** Sher Shah = "RRR" — Rupiya, Roads (GT Road), Revenue reforms.

**TL;DR**

- Humayun lost to Sher Shah at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540), then was exiled to Safavid Persia.
- He recaptured Delhi in 1555 and died in 1556; Humayun's Tomb is India's first garden tomb.
- Sher Shah Suri (Farid Khan) founded the Sur dynasty and ruled 1540-45.
- His rise: born **Farid Khan** into an **Afghan** family at **Sasaram in Bihar**, he earned the title **'Sher Khan'** for killing a tiger, and founded the Sur dynasty after defeating Humayun at Kannauj (1540).
- His reforms — rupiya, GT Road, patta/kabuliyat, dagh & chehra — became the base for Akbar's administration.
keyPoints: Humayun lost to Sher Shah at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540), then exiled to Safavid Persia.
He recaptured Delhi in 1555 and died in 1556; Humayun's Tomb is India's first garden tomb.
Sher Shah Suri (Farid Khan) founded the Sur dynasty and ruled 1540-45.
Sher Shah's revenue: sarkar/pargana units, one-third produce, patta and kabuliyat to peasants.
He introduced the silver rupiya and copper dam, revived the Grand Trunk Road with sarais, and used dagh & chehra.
Sher Shah's original name was Farid Khan; born to an Afghan family at Sasaram (Bihar); title 'Sher Khan' for killing a tiger.

items.title: Akbar the Great (1556-1605): Conquests, Religion & Administration
items.body:
**In one line:** Akbar (ruled 1556-1605) built the Mughal Empire's lasting strength by combining military conquest, religious tolerance, and systematic administration.

**The story**

- **Jalal-ud-din Akbar** came to the throne aged 13 (thirteen) in **1556** under the regent **Bairam Khan**, who won the **Second Battle of Panipat (1556)** against **Hemu**.
- He expanded through campaigns such as the **Siege of Chittorgarh (1567-68)**, **Haldighati (1576)** against **Maharana Pratap of Mewar** (Mughal army led by **Man Singh**), and the annexation of **Gujarat (1573)** and **Bengal (1576)**.
- In religion he abolished the **jizya**, promoted **Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace)**, debated faiths at the **Ibadat Khana**, and founded the syncretic **Din-i-Ilahi (1582)** (few followers).
- For administration he built two famous systems — the **Dahsala/Zabti** revenue system (with **Raja Todar Mal**) and the **Mansabdari** rank system — that bound nobles to the emperor and gave the treasury stability.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** Mansabdari (Zat/Sawar), Dahsala, Sulh-i-Kul, Din-i-Ilahi and the Navaratnas are among the highest-frequency Mughal exam points.

**Picture it — Akbar's two key systems**

| System | What it did |
|---|---|
| **Dahsala / Zabti** (Todar Mal's Bandobast) | Revenue fixed on the **average produce & prices of 10 years**; state share one-third. Alternatives: Batai/Ghalla-Bakshi, Kankut |
| **Mansabdari** | Every officer held a **mansab (rank)** with two numbers — **Zat** (personal status/pay) and **Sawar** (cavalry to maintain); ranks 10 up to 5,000 (7,000 for princes) |

**Terms explained**

- **jizya** = a tax that had been levied on non-Muslims; Akbar abolished it.
- **Sulh-i-Kul** = "peace with all", Akbar's policy of treating all religions equally.
- **Din-i-Ilahi** = Akbar's blended "religion of God" (1582), drawing from several faiths.
- **Zat / Sawar** = the two numbers of a mansab — Zat = rank/status, Sawar = number of horsemen to keep.
- **Navaratnas** = Akbar's "nine gems" (notably **Todar Mal, Abul Fazl, Tansen, Birbal, Man Singh, Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan, Faizi**); **Abul Fazl** wrote the **Akbarnama**, whose third volume is the **Ain-i-Akbari**.

**Who did what among the Navaratnas**

| Navaratna | Role |
| --- | --- |
| Todar Mal | Finance minister; revenue reforms (Dahsala) |
| Abul Fazl | Author of the Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari |
| Tansen | Renowned court musician |
| Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan | Poet who translated the Baburnama into Persian |
| Birbal | Witty courtier and adviser |

**Don't confuse:** **Zat vs Sawar** — Zat is personal status, Sawar is the cavalry quota. The **Akbarnama** is the history; its **third volume**, the **Ain-i-Akbari**, is the administrative gazetteer.

**Remember it:** Mansab pair = "Zat = self, Sawar = soldiers (horses)."

**TL;DR**

- Akbar acceded 1556; Bairam Khan won Second Panipat against Hemu.
- Conquests: Chittorgarh (1567-68), Haldighati (1576), Gujarat (1573), Bengal (1576).
- Religion: abolished jizya, promoted Sulh-i-Kul, founded Din-i-Ilahi (1582).
- Dahsala/Zabti fixed revenue on 10-year averages; Mansabdari ranks had Zat and Sawar; Abul Fazl wrote the Akbarnama (Ain-i-Akbari).
keyPoints: Akbar acceded in 1556; Bairam Khan won the Second Battle of Panipat against Hemu.

Religious policy: abolished jizya, promoted Sulh-i-Kul, founded Din-i-Ilahi (1582).
Dahsala/Zabti (Todar Mal's Bandobast) fixed revenue on 10-year average produce, one-third share.
Mansabdari ranks had Zat (status) and Sawar (cavalry) components.
Abul Fazl wrote the Akbarnama; its third volume is the Ain-i-Akbari.

items.title: Jahangir & Shah Jahan: Nur Jahan, English Contact & the Architectural Peak
items.body:
**In one line:** Under Jahangir and Shah Jahan the Mughal court reached its cultural and architectural peak — Nur Jahan's political power, the first English contacts, and the Taj Mahal all belong here.

**The story**

- Prince **Salim** took the title **Jahangir** ("world-seizer") in **1605**. In 1611 he married **Mehr-un-Nisa (Nur Jahan)**, whose faction (the "Nur Jahan Junta") dominated the court.
- English contact grew: Captain Hawkins visited, **Sir Thomas Roe** (envoy of James I, 1615-19) secured trading rights, and the English set up their **first factory at Surat (1613)**. Jahangir lost **Qandahar** to Persia (1622) and was known for the **Zanjir-i-Adl (chain of justice)** at Agra Fort.
- Prince **Khurram**, titled **Shah Jahan** (ruled **1628-1658**), built the **Taj Mahal** for **Mumtaz Mahal (Arjumand Banu)**, who died in 1631. His reign is the **golden age of Mughal architecture**.
- When he fell ill in 1657, a **war of succession** broke out among his sons; **Aurangzeb** won and imprisoned him in **Agra Fort** until his death in **1666**.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** Nur Jahan, Thomas Roe/Surat 1613, the Taj Mahal and the Peacock Throne are repeated match and date questions.

**Picture it**

| Ruler | Reign | Remember for |
|---|---|---|
| Jahangir (Salim) | 1605-1627 | Nur Jahan; Thomas Roe & Surat factory (1613); chain of justice |
| Shah Jahan (Khurram) | 1628-1658 | Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Peacock Throne |

**Terms explained**

- **Zanjir-i-Adl** = a "chain of justice" with bells, which any subject could pull to seek the emperor's hearing.
- **factory** = a fortified trading warehouse of the East India Company (not a modern mill).
- **Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus)** = Shah Jahan's jewelled imperial throne.
- **Mumtaz Mahal** = Shah Jahan's queen (Arjumand Banu); the Taj Mahal is her tomb.

**Don't confuse:** **Jahangir = Prince Salim; Shah Jahan = Prince Khurram.** The **first English factory (Surat, 1613)** came slightly *before* Thomas Roe's embassy (1615-19), which then won formal trading rights.

**Remember it:** "Salim → Jahangir → Nur Jahan; Khurram → Shah Jahan → Taj Mahal."

**TL;DR**

- Jahangir (Prince Salim) married Nur Jahan (1611), who held major political influence.
- Sir Thomas Roe secured trading rights; the English set up their first factory at Surat in 1613.
- Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal for Mumtaz Mahal and the Peacock Throne — the architectural golden age.
- Aurangzeb won the war of succession and imprisoned Shah Jahan in Agra Fort till 1666.
keyPoints: Jahangir (Prince Salim) married Nur Jahan (1611), who wielded major political influence.
Sir Thomas Roe secured trading rights; the English set up their first factory at Surat in 1613.
Jahangir was known for the chain of justice (Zanjir-i-Adl) at Agra Fort.
Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal for Mumtaz Mahal and the Peacock Throne.
His reign is the golden age of Mughal architecture (Red Fort, Jama Masjid).
Aurangzeb won the war of succession and imprisoned Shah Jahan in Agra Fort till 1666.

items.title: Aurangzeb & the Decline of the Mughal Empire
items.body:
**In one line:** The empire reached its largest size under Aurangzeb, but his religious orthodoxy, endless Deccan wars, and later weak successors led to rapid decline.

**The story**

- **Aurangzeb Alamgir** (ruled **1658-1707**) won a **war of succession** against **Dara Shikoh**, imprisoned Shah Jahan, and ruled as an orthodox Sunni nicknamed **'Zinda Pir' (living saint)**.
- His **religious measures** — re-imposing **jizya in 1679**, appointing **muhtasibs (moral police)**, ending court music, and executing **Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675)** — alienated Hindus, Rajputs and Sikhs.
- In the **Deccan** he annexed **Bijapur and Golconda (1686-87)** — bringing Andhra's Qutb Shahi Golconda under Mughal rule — but decades of costly war against the **Marathas (Shivaji, Sambhaji)** drained the treasury (the "Deccan ulcer"). The empire reached its **greatest extent** yet was overstretched. He died at **Ahmednagar in 1707**.
- Afterwards, weak successors became **puppets of nobles**; the empire fractured.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** The "peak-yet-decline" paradox, jizya 1679, Nadir Shah 1739 and the break-away provinces are classic Prelims and Mains material.

**Picture it — causes of decline**

| Type | Factors |
|---|---|
| Aurangzeb's policies | jizya (1679), orthodoxy, Guru Tegh Bahadur's execution, the Deccan ulcer |
| Structural | empty treasury, jagirdari crisis, Irani-Turani factionalism, weak successors |
| External shocks | **Nadir Shah** sacked Delhi (**1739, Battle of Karnal**), took the Peacock Throne & Koh-i-Noor; **Ahmad Shah Abdali** raided 1748-61 |
| Break-away provinces | Hyderabad (Asaf Jahi/Nizam), Bengal (Murshid Quli Khan), Awadh |

**Terms explained**

- **jizya** = the tax on non-Muslims that Akbar had abolished and Aurangzeb re-imposed in 1679.
- **muhtasib** = an official enforcing public morality and Islamic law.
- **jagirdari crisis** = too many nobles competing for too few revenue-assignment lands (jagirs).
- **Sayyid Brothers** = powerful nobles who made and unmade later emperors ("king-makers"), raising and deposing them. **Farrukhsiyar** was the first Mughal emperor to be killed by his own nobles (the Sayyid Brothers, 1719).
- Provinces such as **Hyderabad, Bengal and Awadh** became effectively independent, though they still nominally accepted the emperor.

**Don't confuse:** Aurangzeb's reign was the empire's **largest in area** but the **start of its decline** — size did not mean strength. **Bahadur Shah II** (the last Mughal) was exiled after the **1857 Revolt**, long after real power had gone.

**Remember it:** Aurangzeb = peak size but "Deccan ulcer" + jizya (1679) = seed of decline.

**TL;DR**

- Aurangzeb won the succession war against Dara Shikoh; called Zinda Pir.
- Re-imposed jizya (1679), used muhtasibs, executed Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675).
- Annexed Bijapur and Golconda (1686-87) but exhausted the empire in Deccan/Maratha wars; died 1707.
- Nadir Shah sacked Delhi (1739); provinces (Hyderabad, Bengal, Awadh) broke away; Bahadur Shah II exiled after 1857.
keyPoints: Aurangzeb won the war of succession against Dara Shikoh; called Zinda Pir.
He re-imposed jizya in 1679, appointed muhtasibs, and executed Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675).
Annexed Bijapur and Golconda (1686-87) but exhausted the empire in Deccan/Maratha wars; died 1707.
Nadir Shah sacked Delhi in 1739 (Battle of Karnal), taking the Peacock Throne and Koh-i-Noor.
Later Mughals were puppets of nobles like the Sayyid Brothers; provinces (Hyderabad, Bengal, Awadh) broke away.
Bahadur Shah II, the last Mughal, was exiled to Rangoon after the 1857 Revolt.

Signature policies recap: Akbar — Sulh-i-Kul (peace with all); Jahangir — hung the Zanjir-i-Adl (chain of justice) at Agra Fort; Aurangzeb — executed Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Sikh Guru (1675); Bahadur Shah II — exiled to Rangoon after the 1857 Revolt.

items.title: The Marathas: Shivaji & the Peshwas
items.body:
**In one line:** The Marathas, led first by Chhatrapati Shivaji and later by the Peshwas, rose as the great power that challenged and outlasted the Mughals in the Deccan.

**The story**

- **Chhatrapati Shivaji** (1630-1680), born at **Shivneri Fort** and inspired by his mother **Jijabai** and guardian **Dadoji Kondadeo**, coined the ideal of **'Hindavi Swarajya'** (self-rule).
- He rose against **Bijapur** — killing **Afzal Khan** at **Pratapgarh (1659)** — raided **Surat (1664)**, signed the **Treaty of Purandar (1665)** with Jai Singh, and escaped from Agra (1666).
- Crowned **Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674**, he was a master of **guerrilla warfare**, held hundreds of forts, built a navy, and ran the state through the **Ashtapradhan** (council of eight ministers). He levied **Chauth** (one-fourth of revenue) and **Sardeshmukhi** (an extra one-tenth) on neighbouring lands.
- After Shivaji and **Sambhaji** (executed by Aurangzeb, 1689), real power passed to the **Peshwas**: **Shahu** appointed **Balaji Vishwanath** Peshwa in **1713**. The Marathas expanded until the disastrous **Third Battle of Panipat (1761)** loss to **Ahmad Shah Abdali**.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** Shivaji's coronation, Ashtapradhan, Chauth/Sardeshmukhi and Panipat 1761 are high-frequency facts and link directly to Mughal decline.

**Picture it — Maratha landmarks**

| Event | Year |
|---|---|
| Killed Afzal Khan (Pratapgarh) | 1659 |
| Raided Surat | 1664 |
| Treaty of Purandar | 1665 |
| Crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad | 1674 |
| Balaji Vishwanath made Peshwa | 1713 |
| Third Battle of Panipat (vs Abdali) | 1761 |

**Terms explained**

- **Hindavi Swarajya** = Shivaji's idea of self-rule for the people of the land.
- **Ashtapradhan** = Shivaji's "council of eight" ministers, headed by the **Peshwa** (prime minister).
- **Chauth** = a tax of one-fourth of revenue; **Sardeshmukhi** = an extra one-tenth, levied on lands outside the kingdom.
- **Peshwa** = the Maratha prime minister; after 1713 the Peshwas became the real rulers.

**Don't confuse:** **Chauth = 1/4, Sardeshmukhi = extra 1/10** (not the other way round). The **Third** Panipat (1761) was Marathas vs Abdali — not Babur or Akbar.

**Remember it:** Maratha taxes = "Chauth = 1/4, Sardeshmukhi = extra 1/10."

**TL;DR**

- Shivaji coined 'Hindavi Swarajya' and was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674.
- He killed Afzal Khan at Pratapgarh (1659), raided Surat (1664), signed the Treaty of Purandar (1665).
- Ashtapradhan was his council of eight ministers headed by the Peshwa; Chauth (1/4) and Sardeshmukhi (extra 1/10) were the taxes.
- Shahu made Balaji Vishwanath Peshwa in 1713; the Marathas lost the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) to Abdali.
keyPoints: Shivaji coined 'Hindavi Swarajya' and was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674.

Ashtapradhan was Shivaji's council of eight ministers headed by the Peshwa.
Chauth (1/4 of revenue) and Sardeshmukhi (extra 1/10) were the Maratha taxes.
Shahu made Balaji Vishwanath Peshwa in 1713, beginning the Peshwa era.
The Marathas lost the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) to Ahmad Shah Abdali.

items.title: Babur and Humayun in Detail — Dates, Places, Buildings and Chroniclers
items.body:
### Babur and Humayun in Detail — Dates, Places, Buildings and Chroniclers

**In one line**
Beyond 'Panipat 1526' and 'Chausa 1539', exams ask who invited Babur, where Khanwa was fought, where he lies buried, and who designed and wrote about Humayun's world.

**The story**
Babur was born at **Andijan** in **1483** and inherited Ferghana from **Umar Sheikh Mirza**. **Daulat Khan Lodi** of Punjab invited him. He won Panipat on **21 April** 1526 and **Khanwa** near **Fatehpur Sikri** (1527), after which he called himself **Ghazi**, then beat **Mahmud Lodi** at Ghaghra. His noble **Mir Baqi** built the mosque at **Ayodhya**; he laid out **Aram Bagh**; and he lies at **Bagh-e-Babur** in **Kabul**. Humayun besieged **Kalinjar** (1531), won at **Dadrah**, chased **Bahadur Shah** of Gujarat to **Diu**, and after Chausa was saved by the **water-carrier** **Nizam**. He built **Din-panah**, came back by winning at **Sirhind** (1555) against **Sikandar** Suri, and died falling down the **Sher Mandal** stairs. **Mirak Mirza Ghiyas** designed his tomb for **Bega Begum**; **Gulbadan Begum** and **Khwandamir** wrote about him.

#### Babur

| Point | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Birth** | 1483 | Born at **Andijan** (Ferghana) |
| **Ferghana throne** | 1494 | Succeeded his father **Umar Sheikh Mirza** aged about 11 |
| **Invitation** | c.1524 | **Daulat Khan Lodi** (Punjab governor) and Rana Sanga invited Babur |
| **First Panipat** | 21 April 1526 | Ibrahim Lodi killed; artillery under Ustad Ali and Mustafa |
| **Khanwa** | 17 March 1527 | Near **Fatehpur Sikri**; Babur took the title **Ghazi** |
| **Ghaghra** | 6 May 1529 | Afghans under **Mahmud Lodi** defeated (Bihar) |
| **Death and burial** | 1530 | Died at Agra (his capital); reburied at **Bagh-e-Babur**, **Kabul** |
| **Babri Masjid** | 1528 | Built at **Ayodhya** by **Mir Baqi**, a Babur noble |
| **Aram Bagh** | — | Ram Bagh, Agra — one of the earliest Mughal charbagh gardens |

#### Humayun

| Point | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Kalinjar** | 1531 | Six-month siege in Bundelkhand; the raja paid compensation |
| **Dadrah** | 1532 | Afghans defeated near the Gomti |
| **Bahadur Shah of Gujarat** | 1535–36 | Lost Mandu and Champaner; fled to **Diu** with Portuguese help; regained Gujarat in 1536 |
| **Nizam the water-carrier** | 1539 | Saved Humayun at Chausa; sat on the throne for a short while as reward |
| **Machhiwara & Sirhind** | 1555 | Beat **Sikandar** Shah Suri at **Sirhind** (22 June 1555); recovered Delhi |
| **Din-panah** | 1533 | His city at Delhi; Sher Shah rebuilt it as Purana Qila |
| **Death** | 1556 | Fell from the stairs of his library, the **Sher Mandal** |
| **Humayun's Tomb** | 1560s–1572 | Architect **Mirak Mirza Ghiyas**; built by widow **Bega Begum**; double dome, charbagh |
| **Humayun-nama** | c.1587 | By **Gulbadan Begum**, Humayun's half-sister |
| **Khwandamir** | 1530s | Chronicler of Humayun's early reign (Qanun-i-Humayuni) |

**Don't confuse**
- Babur's capital was **Agra**; the source PDF's 'Babur established Delhi as capital' is loose — he held both, but ruled and died at Agra.
- Khanwa is dated 16 or 17 March 1527 in different books; the source PDF itself gives both. Chanderi is dated 20 or 29 January 1528.
- **Humayun-nama** (Gulbadan Begum) ≠ **Akbarnama** (Abul Fazl).

**TL;DR**
- Babur: Andijan 1483; invited by Daulat Khan Lodi; Panipat 21 April 1526; Khanwa near Fatehpur Sikri (Ghazi); Ghaghra vs Mahmud Lodi; buried Bagh-e-Babur, Kabul.
- Humayun: Kalinjar 1531, Dadrah 1532, Bahadur Shah fled to Diu; Nizam the water-carrier; Din-panah; Sirhind 1555; died at Sher Mandal.
- Humayun's Tomb — Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, Bega Begum; Humayun-nama — Gulbadan Begum.
keyPoints: Babur was born at Andijan (1483) and was invited by Daulat Khan Lodi, governor of Punjab.
Khanwa (1527) was fought near Fatehpur Sikri, after which Babur took the title Ghazi; he is buried at Bagh-e-Babur, Kabul.
Humayun chased Bahadur Shah of Gujarat to Diu and was saved at Chausa by Nizam the water-carrier.
Humayun recovered Delhi by defeating Sikandar Shah Suri at Sirhind (1555) and died falling from the Sher Mandal library stairs (1556).
Humayun's Tomb was designed by Mirak Mirza Ghiyas for Bega Begum; Gulbadan Begum wrote the Humayun-nama.

items.title: The Sur Dynasty in Detail — Sher Shah's Officials, Roads, Buildings and Successors
items.body:
### The Sur Dynasty in Detail — Sher Shah's Officials, Roads, Buildings and Successors

**In one line**
Sher Shah ruled only five years (1540–45), but exams test his officials by name, his roads and buildings, how he died and who followed him.

**The story**
Sher Shah won Bihar at **Surajgarh** (1534) and died at the siege of **Kalinjar** in **1545**. He split his empire into **47** sarkars, run by a **Shiqdar**-i-Shiqdaran and a **Munsif**-i-Munsifan; in each pargana the Amin, **Fotedar** and **Karkun** handled revenue, treasure and accounts. Land was graded good, **middling** and bad. His great road ran from **Sonargaon** to **Peshawar**. He built **Rohtas** Fort, the **Qila-i-Kuhna** mosque, and his tomb at **Sasaram** in a **lake**; **Jayasi** wrote the **Padmavat** in his time. His son **Islam Shah** ruled until 1553; then **Muhammad Adil** Shah, whose minister was **Hemu**, took over before Humayun's return. Humayun called him a **teacher of kings**.

#### Sher Shah and the Sur kings

| Item | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Surajgarh** | 1534 | Beat the Lohanis and Mahmud Shah of Bengal; took Bihar |
| **Death** | 1545 | Killed by a gunpowder blast at the siege of **Kalinjar** |
| **47 sarkars** | — | Empire divided into **47** sarkars, each split into parganas |
| **Shiqdar / Munsif** | — | **Shiqdar**-i-Shiqdaran = law and order; **Munsif**-i-Munsifan = revenue and civil justice |
| **Amin, Fotedar, Karkun** | — | Amin = revenue assessor; **Fotedar** = treasurer; **Karkun** = accountant |
| **Land classes** | — | Good, **middling** and bad; state share one-third of the average |
| **Grand Trunk Road** | — | Sadak-i-Azam from **Sonargaon** to **Peshawar** (PDF: Chittagong to Kabul); sarais every few miles |
| **Rohtas Fort** | — | In Punjab (now Pakistan); built to check the Gakhars |
| **Sasaram tomb** | — | Octagonal tomb in the middle of a **lake**, Bihar |
| **Qila-i-Kuhna mosque** | — | In the Purana Qila, Delhi |
| **Padmavat** | 1540 | Hindi (Awadhi) epic by **Malik Muhammad Jayasi** |
| **Islam Shah** | 1545–1553 | Sher Shah's son; strict army discipline |
| **Muhammad Adil Shah** | 1553–1555 | Killed the boy Firoz Shah; his general-minister was **Hemu** |
| **Teacher of kings** | — | Humayun is said to have called Sher Shah the 'teacher of kings' (Ustad-i-Badshahan) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Shiqdar** (law and order) ≠ **Munsif** (revenue/justice) ≠ **Amin** (assessor).
- The PDF says the GT Road ran from Chittagong to Kabul; standard books give **Sonargaon to Peshawar** (later extended).
- **Hemu** served the Sur king Muhammad Adil Shah, then fought Akbar at Second Panipat.

**TL;DR**
- Surajgarh 1534; died at Kalinjar 1545 (gunpowder blast).
- 47 sarkars; Shiqdar & Munsif; Amin, Fotedar, Karkun; land good/middling/bad.
- Road Sonargaon–Peshawar; Rohtas Fort; Sasaram tomb in a lake; Jayasi — Padmavat.
- Successors: Islam Shah (1545–53), Muhammad Adil Shah (minister Hemu).
keyPoints: Sher Shah won Bihar at Surajgarh (1534) and died at the siege of Kalinjar (1545).
His empire had 47 sarkars; the Shiqdar-i-Shiqdaran kept order and the Munsif-i-Munsifan handled revenue; the Fotedar was treasurer and the Karkun accountant.
His road ran from Sonargaon to Peshawar; he built Rohtas Fort and a tomb at Sasaram in a lake.
Malik Muhammad Jayasi wrote the Padmavat in his time.
Islam Shah succeeded him; Hemu was minister of Muhammad Adil Shah Sur.

items.title: Akbar in Detail — Regency, Religious Steps, Revenue Terms, Officials and Court Culture
items.body:
### Akbar in Detail — Regency, Religious Steps, Revenue Terms, Officials and Court Culture

**In one line**
Akbar's reign carries more exam terms than any other: the steps of his religious policy with years, the land classes, the central officers, and who wrote or painted at his court.

**The story**
Born at **Umarkot** (**1542**), Akbar beat **Hemu**, who had styled himself **Vikramaditya**. He dropped **Bairam Khan** in **1560**; then came the '**petticoat** government' of **Maham Anaga**. He ended the **pilgrim tax** and the jizya (**1564**), built the **Ibadat Khana** (**1575**) and issued the **Mahzar** (**1579**). Fatehpur Sikri honoured **Salim Chishti**. He took **Kashmir** (1586) and finally **Asirgarh**. In revenue, **karori**s came in 1574 and the Dahsala in **1580**; land was **polaj** to **banjar**; **Kankut** and **batai** were alternatives; peasants got **taccavi**; land was **Khalisa** or **jagir** (in lieu of **cash salary**). There were **12** **subas**; the **Mir Bakhshi**, **Sadr-us-Sudur** and **Mir Saman** served at the centre and the **Faujdar** and **Amalguzar** in each sarkar; top mansabs reached **7000**. **Tansen** ('**Mian**'), Birbal (**Mahesh Das**), the **Razmnama**, **Daswanth** and **Basawan**, the **Hamzanama**, **Badauni**, the **Tabaqat-i-Akbari**, the **Tarikh-i-Alfi**, **Monserrate** and **Ralph Fitch** complete the picture.

#### Reign and religious steps

| Point | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Birth** | 1542 | At **Umarkot** (Sindh) during Humayun's flight |
| **Hemu** | 1556 | Sur general; took Delhi and the title **Vikramaditya**; lost Second Panipat |
| **End of regency** | 1560 | **Bairam Khan** dismissed; sent towards Mecca and killed on the way |
| **Petticoat government** | 1560–62 | Influence of foster-mother **Maham Anaga** and her son Adham Khan |
| **Tax abolitions** | 1563–64 | **Pilgrim tax** (1563) and jizya (**1564**) abolished |
| **Ibadat Khana** | 1575 | Hall for debates among faiths at Fatehpur Sikri |
| **Mahzar** | 1579 | Made Akbar Imam-i-Adil, arbiter of religious disputes |
| **Fatehpur Sikri** | 1571–85 | Honoured **Salim Chishti**; Buland Darwaza marks the Gujarat victory |
| **Asirgarh** | 1601 | Akbar's last conquest (Khandesh) |
| **Kashmir** | 1586 | Annexed |

#### Revenue terms and officials

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Karori** | 1574 — officials appointed to collect a crore of dams and check local figures |
| **Dahsala** | Introduced **1580** — ten-year average of produce and prices |
| **Polaj / parauti / chachar / banjar** | **Polaj** = every year; parauti = fallow 1–2 years; chachar = 3–4 years; **banjar** = 5+ years |
| **Kankut / batai** | **Kankut** = estimate of the standing crop; **batai** = crop-sharing after harvest |
| **Taccavi** | Loans to peasants for seed, cattle and tools |
| **Khalisa** | Crown land — revenue straight to the treasury (vs jagir) |
| **Jagir** | Revenue assignment in lieu of a **cash salary**; the jagirdar did not own the land |
| **Subas** | **12** **subas** (provinces), later 15 |
| **Mir Bakhshi** | Head of the military department and mansabdari |
| **Sadr-us-Sudur** | Religious affairs and charitable grants |
| **Mir Saman** | Imperial household and karkhanas (workshops) |
| **Faujdar / Amalguzar** | **Faujdar** = law and order; **Amalguzar** = revenue (sarkar level) |
| **Top mansab** | Raised from 5000 to **7000** for nobles |

#### Court culture and visitors

| Person / work | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Tansen** | Musician titled '**Mian**'; earlier at Rewa |
| **Birbal** | **Mahesh Das**; killed fighting the Yusufzais (1586) |
| **Razmnama** | Persian Mahabharata (Faizi, Badauni and others) |
| **Daswanth, Basawan** | Akbar's leading painters; studio under Abdus Samad and Mir Sayyid Ali |
| **Hamzanama** | First great illustrated work of the Mughal studio |
| **Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh** | By **Badauni** — critical of Akbar's religious policy |
| **Tabaqat-i-Akbari** | By Nizamuddin Ahmad |
| **Tarikh-i-Alfi** | History of 1,000 years of Islam, by several authors |
| **Monserrate** | Jesuit at Akbar's court (1578–82) |
| **Ralph Fitch** | English merchant (1585–91) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Khalisa** (crown land) ≠ **jagir** (assigned revenue) ≠ **inam** (charity grant).
- **Polaj** = cultivated every year; **banjar** = uncultivated 5+ years.
- **Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh** (Badauni, critical) ≠ **Akbarnama** (Abul Fazl, official).

**TL;DR**
- Umarkot 1542; Hemu = Vikramaditya; Bairam Khan out 1560; petticoat government (Maham Anaga).
- Pilgrim tax 1563, jizya 1564, Ibadat Khana 1575, Mahzar 1579, Din-i-Ilahi 1582.
- Karori 1574, Dahsala 1580; polaj/parauti/chachar/banjar; kankut, batai, taccavi; khalisa vs jagir.
- Mir Bakhshi, Sadr-us-Sudur, Mir Saman; Faujdar & Amalguzar; 12 subas.
- Razmnama; Daswanth, Basawan; Hamzanama; Badauni; Monserrate; Ralph Fitch.
keyPoints: Hemu took the title Vikramaditya; Akbar dismissed Bairam Khan in 1560; Maham Anaga's dominance is called the 'petticoat government'.
Akbar abolished the pilgrim tax (1563) and jizya (1564), built the Ibadat Khana (1575) and issued the Mahzar (1579).
Land classes: polaj, parauti, chachar, banjar; khalisa was crown land; a jagir was given instead of a cash salary.
The Mir Bakhshi headed the military; the Faujdar kept order and the Amalguzar collected revenue in a sarkar.
The Razmnama is the Persian Mahabharata; Badauni's Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh criticises Akbar.

items.title: Jahangir and Shah Jahan in Detail — Revolts, Visitors, Painters, Buildings and Chronicles
items.body:
### Jahangir and Shah Jahan in Detail — Revolts, Visitors, Painters, Buildings and Chronicles

**In one line**
The middle Mughal age is tested through names: who rebelled, which Guru was executed, which Englishmen came, which painter drew birds, which tomb first used pietra dura, and who wrote the Padshahnama.

**The story**
Jahangir faced **Khusrau**'s revolt in **1606** and executed Guru **Arjan** Dev. **Hawkins** came in 1608; at **Swally** **Thomas Best** beat the Portuguese. He wrote the **Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri**; **Ustad Mansur** painted birds and **Bishandas** portraits. Nur Jahan built **Itimad-ud-Daulah**'s tomb with **pietra dura**; Jahangir completed Akbar's tomb at **Sikandra** and laid out **Shalimar Bagh** in **Kashmir**. Shah Jahan beat **Shahryar** and was crowned in **1628**; **Ustad Ahmad Lahori** led work on the Taj; **Shahjahanabad** was finished in **1648**; **Bebadal Khan** made the Peacock Throne; **Abdul Hamid Lahori** wrote the **Padshahnama**. He expelled the Portuguese from **Hugli** (**1632**), lost **Qandahar** in **1649** and failed in **Balkh**. His son Dara wrote the **Sirr-i-Akbar** and **Majma-ul-Bahrain** but lost at **Dharmat** and **Samugarh**. **Bernier**, a **physician**, and **Manucci** described the court.

#### Jahangir

| Point | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Khusrau revolt** | 1606 | Jahangir's son rebelled; later blinded |
| **Guru Arjan Dev** | 1606 | Fifth Sikh Guru; executed for blessing Khusrau |
| **William Hawkins** | 1608–11 | English captain; given a mansab |
| **Battle of Swally** | 1612 | English (**Thomas Best**) beat the Portuguese near Surat |
| **Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri** | — | Jahangir's own memoirs in Persian |
| **Ustad Mansur** | — | Painter of birds and animals (Nadir-ul-Asr) |
| **Abul Hasan, Bishandas** | — | Abul Hasan (Nadir-uz-Zaman); **Bishandas** — portraits |
| **Itimad-ud-Daulah tomb** | 1622–28 | Built by Nur Jahan; first white-marble **pietra dura** work |
| **Akbar's tomb** | 1613 | At **Sikandra**, completed by Jahangir |
| **Shalimar Bagh** | 1619 | Garden in **Kashmir** |

#### Shah Jahan and the war of succession

| Point | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Accession** | 1628 | Crowned at Agra after defeating **Shahryar** |
| **Taj Mahal** | 1632–53 | Chief architect **Ustad Ahmad Lahori**; white marble with pietra dura |
| **Shahjahanabad** | 1648 | New capital at Delhi; Red Fort (Lal Qila) and Jama Masjid |
| **Peacock Throne** | 1635 | Made under **Bebadal Khan**; taken by Nadir Shah (1739) |
| **Padshahnama** | — | By **Abdul Hamid Lahori** (official); Inayat Khan wrote the Shah Jahan Nama |
| **Hugli** | 1632 | Portuguese expelled (child-kidnapping and conversion charges) |
| **Qandahar** | 1638 / 1649 | Regained 1638; lost for good in **1649** |
| **Balkh campaign** | 1646–47 | Against the Uzbeks; costly and abandoned |
| **Dara Shikoh** | 1650s | **Sirr-i-Akbar** (50 Upanishads) and **Majma-ul-Bahrain** (meeting of two oceans) |
| **Samugarh** | 1658 | Decisive defeat of Dara; **Dharmat** (vs Jaswant Singh) came first |
| **Travellers** | 1650s–80s | Tavernier & **Bernier** (France), **Manucci** (Italy), Peter Mundy (England) |
| **François Bernier** | 1656–68 | French **physician**; 'Travels in the Mughal Empire' |

**Don't confuse**
- **Guru Arjan Dev** (5th) was executed by **Jahangir** (1606); **Guru Tegh Bahadur** (9th) by **Aurangzeb** (1675).
- **Itimad-ud-Daulah** (Nur Jahan, first white-marble pietra dura) ≠ **Taj Mahal** (Shah Jahan).
- The source PDF says Shah Jahan 'took Qandahar back' (1638); it was lost for good in 1649.

**TL;DR**
- Khusrau revolt 1606; Guru Arjan Dev executed 1606; Hawkins; Swally 1612 (Thomas Best).
- Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri; Ustad Mansur (birds), Bishandas (portraits); Itimad-ud-Daulah (pietra dura); Sikandra; Shalimar Bagh.
- Shah Jahan: 1628; Ustad Ahmad Lahori (Taj); Shahjahanabad 1648; Bebadal Khan; Padshahnama (Abdul Hamid Lahori); Hugli 1632; Qandahar lost 1649.
- Dara: Sirr-i-Akbar, Majma-ul-Bahrain; lost at Dharmat and Samugarh (1658). Bernier (physician), Manucci.
keyPoints: Jahangir crushed the revolt of Khusrau (1606) and executed Guru Arjan Dev.
Hawkins visited Jahangir; Thomas Best beat the Portuguese at Swally (1612); Jahangir wrote the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri.
Ustad Mansur painted birds and animals; Nur Jahan's tomb for Itimad-ud-Daulah first used pietra dura in white marble.
Ustad Ahmad Lahori is credited with the Taj Mahal; Shahjahanabad was completed in 1648; Abdul Hamid Lahori wrote the Padshahnama.
Dara Shikoh wrote the Sirr-i-Akbar and Majma-ul-Bahrain and lost to Aurangzeb at Samugarh (1658).

items.title: Aurangzeb in Detail and the Later Mughals — Rulers, Revolts and Successor States
items.body:
### Aurangzeb in Detail and the Later Mughals — Rulers, Revolts and Successor States

**In one line**
Aurangzeb's 49 years and the 150 years after him are tested through rulers' nicknames, revolts, chronicles and the governors who turned their provinces into kingdoms.

**The story**
As **Alamgir**, Aurangzeb banned **Nauroz** and the **jharokha** darshan and had the **Fatawa-i-Alamgiri** compiled; Saqi Mustaid Khan wrote the **Maasir-i-Alamgiri**. His son built the **Bibi-ka-Maqbara**, the **Taj of the Deccan**; he built the **Badshahi Mosque**. **Lachit** beat his army at **Saraighat**; **Shaista Khan** took **Chittagong**; **Gokula**'s Jats, the **Satnamis** and **Durgadas** rose. He lies at **Khuldabad**. **Bahadur Shah I** freed **Shahu**; **Jahandar Shah** began **ijara**; **Farrukhsiyar** issued the **1717** farman; **Muhammad Shah** was '**Rangeela**'; **Abdali** invaded from **1748**; **Alamgir II** reigned at **Plassey**; **Shah Alam II** signed at **Allahabad**; **Akbar II** made **Rammohan** a Raja; **Bahadur Shah II** died at **Rangoon** in **1862**. Meanwhile **Saadat Khan** (**Awadh**), **Murshid Quli Khan** (**Murshidabad**), Sawai **Jai Singh** (**Jantar Mantar**), **Suraj Mal** (**Bharatpur**), **Martanda Varma** (**Travancore**) and the Rohillas (**Rohilkhand**) built their own states.

#### Aurangzeb

| Point | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Alamgir** | 1658 | His imperial title — 'world-conqueror' |
| **Court customs ended** | 1660s | **Nauroz**, tuladan (weighing) and **jharokha** darshan stopped; court singing banned |
| **Fatawa-i-Alamgiri** | — | Digest of Hanafi law compiled under Aurangzeb |
| **Maasir-i-Alamgiri** | — | By Saqi Mustaid Khan; Ishwardas Nagar wrote Futuhat-i-Alamgiri |
| **Bibi-ka-Maqbara** | 1660s | Aurangabad; by Azam Shah for his mother — '**Taj of the Deccan**' |
| **Badshahi Mosque / Moti Masjid** | 1673 / 1659 | Lahore; Moti Masjid in the Delhi Red Fort |
| **Saraighat** | 1671 | **Lachit** Borphukan (Ahom) beat the Mughals on the Brahmaputra |
| **Chittagong** | 1666 | **Shaista Khan** defeated the Magh pirates |
| **Jat & Satnami revolts** | 1669 / 1672 | Jats under **Gokula** (Mathura); **Satnamis** (Narnaul) |
| **Durgadas Rathore** | 1679–1707 | Led Marwar resistance; backed prince Akbar's revolt (1681) |
| **Death** | 1707 | Died at Ahmednagar; simple grave at **Khuldabad** |

#### Later Mughals and successor states

| Ruler / state | Years | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Bahadur Shah I** | 1707–1712 | Muazzam/Shah Alam I; released **Shahu** |
| **Jahandar Shah** | 1712–1713 | Introduced **ijara** (revenue farming) |
| **Farrukhsiyar** | 1713–1719 | **1717** farman — duty-free English trade in Bengal; killed by the Sayyids |
| **Muhammad Shah** | 1719–1748 | '**Rangeela**'; Nadir Shah's invasion (1739) |
| **Ahmad Shah Abdali** | 1748–1767 | Afghan; repeated invasions (PDF: five, 1748–61) |
| **Alamgir II** | 1754–1759 | Emperor at **Plassey** (1757); murdered |
| **Shah Alam II** | 1759–1806 | Buxar 1764; Treaty of **Allahabad** 1765 (Diwani to the Company) |
| **Akbar II** | 1806–1837 | Gave **Rammohan** Roy the title 'Raja' |
| **Bahadur Shah II** | 1837–1857 | Last emperor; exiled to **Rangoon**, died **1862** |
| **Awadh** | 1722 | **Saadat Khan** Burhan-ul-Mulk; successor Safdar Jang |
| **Bengal** | 1717 | **Murshid Quli Khan**; capital **Murshidabad** |
| **Sawai Jai Singh** | 1727 | Founded Jaipur; **Jantar Mantar** observatories at five places |
| **Jats** | 1750s | **Bharatpur** at its height under **Suraj Mal** |
| **Travancore** | 1729 | **Martanda Varma** (defeated the Dutch at Colachel, 1741) |
| **Rohilkhand** | 1740s | Afghan Rohilla state of Ali Muhammad Khan |

**Don't confuse**
- **Bibi-ka-Maqbara** ('Taj of the Deccan', Aurangabad) ≠ **Ibrahim Rauza** (Bijapur) ≠ **Taj Mahal** (Agra).
- The source PDF lists 'Chin Qilich Khan 1748–49' as an emperor and says Guru Gobind Singh exploited Nadir Shah's 1739 raid — both are errors: Chin Qilich Khan was the Nizam, and the Guru died in 1708.
- **Farrukhsiyar's 1717 farman** (Bengal) ≠ the Golconda **Golden Farman** (1632).

**TL;DR**
- Aurangzeb: Alamgir; Nauroz and jharokha ended; Fatawa-i-Alamgiri; Maasir-i-Alamgiri; Bibi-ka-Maqbara; Badshahi Mosque; Saraighat 1671; Chittagong 1666; Gokula, Satnamis, Durgadas; Khuldabad.
- Later Mughals: Bahadur Shah I (Shahu freed), Jahandar Shah (ijara), Farrukhsiyar (1717 farman), Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela', Alamgir II (Plassey), Shah Alam II (Allahabad 1765), Akbar II (Raja Rammohan), Bahadur Shah II (Rangoon 1862).
- Successor states: Awadh (Saadat Khan), Bengal (Murshid Quli Khan), Jaipur (Jai Singh), Bharatpur (Suraj Mal), Travancore (Martanda Varma), Rohilkhand.
keyPoints: Aurangzeb (Alamgir) banned Nauroz and the jharokha darshan; the Fatawa-i-Alamgiri was compiled in his reign.
The Bibi-ka-Maqbara at Aurangabad is the 'Taj of the Deccan'; the Ahoms under Lachit Borphukan won at Saraighat (1671).
Jahandar Shah began ijara; Farrukhsiyar's 1717 farman gave the English duty-free trade; Muhammad Shah was called 'Rangeela'.
Shah Alam II signed the Treaty of Allahabad (1765); Akbar II made Rammohan Roy a 'Raja'; Bahadur Shah II died at Rangoon (1862).
Saadat Khan founded Awadh, Murshid Quli Khan made Bengal autonomous, and Sawai Jai Singh built the Jantar Mantar observatories.

items.title: The Marathas in Detail — Shivaji's Campaigns, the Ashtapradhan Posts and the Peshwas
items.body:
### The Marathas in Detail — Shivaji's Campaigns, the Ashtapradhan Posts and the Peshwas

**In one line**
Exams go beyond "1674, Raigad": they match each Ashtapradhan post with its duty, date Shivaji's campaigns, and place each Peshwa and Chhatrapati.

**The story**
Guided by **Dadoji Kondadeo**, Shivaji took **Torna** in **1646**. **Baji Prabhu** held **Pavan Khind** (1660); Shivaji raided Shaista Khan at the **Lal Mahal** (1663), made his **escape** from Agra (**1666**), and his general **Tanaji** won **Sinhagad** (1670) before the open-field victory at **Salher** (1672). He built **Sindhudurg**, revered **Samarth Ramdas**, and fought by **ganimi kava**. His council: **Peshwa** (**prime minister**), **Amatya** (finance), **Sachiv** (letters), **Mantri** (records), **Sumant** (foreign affairs), **Senapati**, **Nyayadhish** and **Panditrao**; Rajaram added the **Pratinidhi**. **Sambhaji** was executed in **1689**; Rajaram held **Gingee**; **Tarabai** ruled from **Kolhapur**; Shahu won at **Khed** and settled at **Warna** (**1731**). **Balaji Vishwanath** helped the **Sayyid** brothers; **Baji Rao I** raided Delhi and took **Bassein**; **Balaji Baji Rao** (**Nana Saheb**) led at Panipat.

#### Shivaji's campaigns

| Event | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Torna** | 1646 | First fort taken, aged about 16 |
| **Dadoji Kondadeo** | — | Guardian who trained him in administration |
| **Pavan Khind** | 1660 | **Baji Prabhu** Deshpande's rearguard; Shivaji escaped Panhala |
| **Night raid on Shaista Khan** | 1663 | Attack at the **Lal Mahal**, Pune |
| **Agra** | 1666 | Placed under house arrest by Aurangzeb; **escape**d with Sambhaji |
| **Sinhagad** | 1670 | **Tanaji** Malusare took Kondhana (renamed **Sinhagad**) |
| **Salher** | 1672 | First major open-field win over the Mughals |
| **Sindhudurg** | 1664–67 | Sea fort and naval base on the Konkan coast |
| **Samarth Ramdas** | — | Spiritual guide (Dasbodh) |
| **Ganimi kava** | — | Guerrilla warfare from hill forts |

#### The Ashtapradhan

| Minister | Duty |
|---|---|
| **Peshwa** | **Prime minister** (Mukhya Pradhan) |
| **Amatya (Mazumdar)** | Finance and revenue |
| **Sachiv (Surnavis)** | Royal correspondence |
| **Mantri (Waqianavis)** | King's daily records and intelligence |
| **Sumant (Dabir)** | Foreign affairs |
| **Senapati** | Army commander |
| **Nyayadhish / Panditrao** | Justice / religious affairs and charity |
| **Pratinidhi** | Added by Rajaram — council became nine |

#### After Shivaji — Chhatrapatis and Peshwas

| Person / event | Years | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Sambhaji** | 1680–1689 | Executed by Aurangzeb in **1689** |
| **Rajaram** | 1689–1700 | Held out at **Gingee** (taken 1698); died at Satara |
| **Tarabai** | 1700–1707 | Regent for Shivaji II; later **Kolhapur** branch |
| **Battle of Khed** | 1707 | Shahu beat Tarabai and took Satara |
| **Treaty of Warna** | 1731 | Settled Satara (Shahu) and Kolhapur |
| **Baji Rao I** | 1720–1740 | Delhi raid 1737; **Bassein** (1739) from the Portuguese; Hindu Pad Padshahi |
| **Balaji Baji Rao** | 1740–1761 | '**Nana Saheb**'; Peshwa at Third Panipat |
| **Balaji Vishwanath** | 1713–1720 | Helped the **Sayyid** brothers (1719); won chauth and sardeshmukhi grants |

**Don't confuse**
- **Amatya** = finance; **Sumant** = foreign affairs; **Sachiv** = correspondence; **Mantri** = daily records.
- **Nana Saheb** here = Peshwa **Balaji Baji Rao** (1740–61), not Nana Saheb of 1857 (Baji Rao II's adopted son).
- The Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775–1818) belong to modern history.

**TL;DR**
- Torna 1646; Pavan Khind 1660; Lal Mahal raid 1663; Agra escape 1666; Sinhagad 1670 (Tanaji); Salher 1672; Sindhudurg; ganimi kava.
- Ashtapradhan: Peshwa (PM), Amatya (finance), Sachiv (letters), Mantri (records), Sumant (foreign), Senapati, Nyayadhish, Panditrao; Pratinidhi added by Rajaram.
- Sambhaji executed 1689; Rajaram at Gingee; Tarabai (Kolhapur); Khed 1707; Warna 1731.
- Balaji Vishwanath (Sayyids 1719), Baji Rao I (Delhi 1737, Bassein 1739), Balaji Baji Rao — Nana Saheb (Panipat 1761).
keyPoints: Shivaji took Torna (1646), escaped from Agra (1666), and Tanaji Malusare won Sinhagad (1670); Salher (1672) was the first big win over the Mughals.
Shivaji built the Sindhudurg sea fort; his guerrilla method is called 'ganimi kava'.
Ashtapradhan: Peshwa — prime minister; Amatya — finance; Sumant — foreign affairs; Rajaram added the Pratinidhi.
Sambhaji was executed in 1689; Rajaram held out at Gingee; the Treaty of Warna (1731) settled the Satara–Kolhapur split.
Baji Rao I raided Delhi (1737) and took Bassein (1739); Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) was Peshwa at Third Panipat.

items.title: For Mains — The Mughal Empire
items.body:
**In one line:** For APPSC Mains Paper-II (medieval India — Mughal administration and culture, Shivaji & the Marathas), the Mughals are the model empire for analysing statecraft, religious policy and the causes of imperial decline.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Administration | Mansabdari (Zat/Sawar), Dahsala/Zabti revenue, Sher Shah's foundations, provincial structure |
| Religious policy | Akbar's Sulh-i-Kul & Din-i-Ilahi vs Aurangzeb's jizya (1679) and orthodoxy — tolerance as statecraft |
| Culture | Indo-Persian synthesis: architecture (Taj, Red Fort), painting, language, Akbarnama/Ain-i-Akbari |
| Economy | Land-revenue as the fiscal base; the jagirdari crisis; trade and the first European factories |
| Significance | Longest-lasting pan-Indian empire; administrative template inherited by the British |
| Decline / criticism | Multi-causal: Deccan ulcer, fiscal exhaustion, factionalism, weak successors, external shocks |

**Data points / names / reports to quote**

- **1526** Panipat; **1556-1605** Akbar; **1679** jizya re-imposed; **1686-87** Bijapur-Golconda annexed; **1707** Aurangzeb's death; **1739** Nadir Shah; **1761** Panipat III.
- **Abul Fazl's Akbarnama / Ain-i-Akbari**; **Todar Mal's** Dahsala; **Sher Shah** as 'Ustad-i-Badshahan'.
- Historiography: the debate on Mughal decline (Satish Chandra's jagirdari crisis; Irfan Habib on the agrarian crisis).

**The AP angle:** Aurangzeb's **annexation of Golconda (1687)** brought the Telugu Qutb Shahi country under the Mughals; the region soon passed to the **Asaf Jahi Nizams of Hyderabad** — a vivid local illustration of imperial overreach.

**Use in answers**

- Example: contrast Akbar's inclusive consolidation with Aurangzeb's orthodoxy to argue that legitimacy, not territory, held the empire together.
- Quote: Humayun's tribute to Sher Shah as 'Teacher of Kings' to open an administration answer.
- Diagram idea: a cause-tree for Mughal decline (policy / structural / external branches).
keyPoints: Mains Paper-II clause (M2-3): Mughal administration & culture; Shivaji & the Marathas.
Frame administration-religion-culture-economy-significance-decline.
Cite Akbarnama/Ain-i-Akbari, Todar Mal's Dahsala, and the decline-debate historiography.
AP angle: Golconda's 1687 annexation and the rise of the Asaf Jahi Nizams of Hyderabad.
